drapeaux.note: L'expression « esprit critique » attribuée à Popper est rendue par « critical spirit » depuis le français ; l'original anglais de Popper est peut-être « critical attitude ». Langue d'origine : français dans la fiche ; auteur : Karl Popper.

accroche: A theory that explains everything, without ever risking anything, may not be a scientific theory.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1919, an expedition led by the British astronomer Arthur Eddington observes a solar eclipse off the coast of Africa and measures the deflection of starlight by the Sun, an effect that general relativity predicted precisely and that Newtonian physics did not predict in the same way. Had the measurement given a different result, Einstein's theory would have been wrong.

That same year, in Vienna, a 17-year-old joins the Marxist movement before breaking away from it, disappointed by its dogmatism; he also immerses himself in the psychoanalysis of Freud and Adler, and will hear Einstein give a lecture on relativity in person. That young man is Karl Popper. What strikes him, over time, is not that Einstein was right. It is the difference in kind between the two approaches.

## The Mechanism

Psychoanalysis and Marxism, Popper notes, have this troubling feature: they explain absolutely everything. An aggressive patient confirms Freudian theory just as much as a submissive one, each through a different mechanism but equally available after the fact. No human observation seems able to catch them out.

General relativity, by contrast, had exposed itself. It predicted a precise figure for the deflection of light, a figure that observation could have contradicted. Had the 1919 eclipse given a different result, the theory would have collapsed on that point alone.

Popper draws a criterion from this. A theory is scientific only if it forbids something, if it takes the risk of being refuted. “All swans are white” is scientific because a single black swan would be enough to refute it. A theory that accommodates any possible result says, at bottom, nothing precise about the world.

This is a reversal of ordinary intuition. We spontaneously believe that a good theory is recognized by what it confirms, by the facts that support it. Popper inverts the criterion: what matters is not what a theory explains. It is what it forbids, and therefore what could, in principle, bring it down.

## What It Shifts

The criterion of falsifiability does not classify psychoanalysis or Marxism as false. It classifies them outside the field whose truth or falsity is settled by observation. Popper speaks of “pre-science” with regard to psychoanalysis, and sees in Marxism a dogma that fell back into pseudo-science. He does not use these words as insults: a theory can be fruitful and rich in meaning without being refutable by a fact.

This shift has a direct consequence for anyone evaluating a claim that presents itself as scientific today. The right question is not “what facts confirm it,” almost always plentiful. It is “what observation, if it occurred, would contradict it.” A theory unable to answer this second question has not yet proven that it belongs to science.

repere.texte: Popper locates the origin of his criterion in the contrast he observes, in Vienna at the turn of the 1920s, between the “critical spirit” of Einstein and its absence in Marx, Freud, and Adler: Freudian theory, he says, was compatible with any possible human observation, whereas Einstein's took the precise risk of being refuted by the 1919 eclipse.
repere.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, entry “Karl Popper”

carte.punch: A theory that explains everything may explain nothing.
carte.idee: Popper notes that Einstein took a precise risk in 1919: the eclipse could have contradicted his theory. Psychoanalysis, by contrast, accommodated any result. Hence his criterion: a theory is scientific only if some fact could, in principle, refute it.

quiz.question: Why does Popper judge that psychoanalysis, as he observes it in Vienna, does not meet his criterion of scientific status?
choix: Because it relies on clinical observations rather than laboratory experiments
Because no human observation seems able to contradict it, whatever behavior is observed
Because it has never been the subject of any attempt at empirical verification
Because its founders did not belong to a recognized scientific discipline
quiz.explication: The problem Popper points to is not a lack of verifications or the clinical origin of the observations: it is that no human behavior, whatever it is, seems able to contradict Freudian theory, each case finding its explanation after the fact. A theory that takes no risk of refutation falls outside the scientific field, according to his criterion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What could have invalidated the theory of general relativity during the 1919 eclipse, according to the card?
choix: Arthur Eddington's refusal to publish his observations
A challenge to the observation method by rival astronomers
A measurement result different from the deflection of light predicted by the theory
The absence of a total eclipse visible from Africa that year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that if the measurement of the deflection of light had given a result different from the one general relativity predicted, Einstein's theory would have been wrong on that point.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Popper characterize psychoanalysis and degenerate Marxism, according to the card?
choix: Two fully fledged scientific disciplines, but less rigorous than physics
Two theories experimentally refuted as early as the 1920s
Two purely religious systems, with no claim to knowledge whatsoever
A pre-science for psychoanalysis, a dogma that fell back into pseudo-science for Marxism
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Popper speaks of pre-science with regard to psychoanalysis, and sees in Marxism a dogma that fell back into pseudo-science, words he does not use as insults, according to the card.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Popper's reversal, how do we recognize a good scientific theory?
choix: By what it forbids, by what could in principle bring it down
By the number of researchers who have validated it by consensus
By its ability to explain a maximum of observed facts
By the age of the discipline it belongs to
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Popper inverts the ordinary intuition that a good theory is recognized by what it confirms: what matters is what it forbids, and therefore what could, in principle, bring it down.
